title: From Shahed to Geran: How Russia Continues to Reinvent the One-Way Attack Drone
gist: Russia has turned Iran's Shahed drone into the continuously-iterated 'Geran' platform via two competing parallel factories (Alabuga and Izhevsk), scaling antenna counts, communications, payloads and airframes on a weeks-long feedback loop that current US acquisition processes cannot match.

themes.theme: Wartime iteration as the core competitive advantage

insights.claim: Russia's Geran drone program demonstrates that modern weapons advantage increasingly comes not from building the most advanced system at the outset, but from maintaining organizational and industrial capacity to continuously iterate a system after it enters combat.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Defense investors should weight production-line flexibility and iteration speed as much as initial platform sophistication when evaluating drone/munitions suppliers.

insights.claim: The feedback loop between battlefield need and delivered engineering change is measured in weeks for Russia's Geran program, not years — one downed Geran had its satellite receiver installed just one week before it was shot down, with no program office in the loop.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: This weeks-long cadence is the benchmark competitors (and US programs) must be measured against; any US drone counter-program running on a multi-year requirements cycle is structurally outmatched.

insights.claim: US programs of record are structured around single primes with formal engineering change proposals required for modifications, meaning US manufacturers cannot iterate on a deployed strike drone at a cadence measured in days or weeks the way Russia's parallel-factory Geran model does.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: This is a structural, not merely budgetary, disadvantage for US drone primes — investors should be skeptical that incremental funding alone (without acquisition-process reform) closes the gap with Russian/Chinese production models.

insights.claim: Russia produces the Geran drone in two parallel factories — Alabuga SEZ in Tatarstan (a repurposed Western-investment zone) and JSC Izhevsk Electromechanical Plant Kupol (a subsidiary of state-owned Almaz-Antey) — which sometimes converge on identical technical solutions and sometimes diverge, suggesting partial but incomplete coordination between the two programs.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Deliberately running redundant, competing production lines on the same weapon platform is a reusable industrial-mobilization model that a wartime US defense-industrial base could emulate for rapid-iteration systems.

insights.claim: Alabuga-built Gerans tend to be scrappier, using ad hoc field modifications (taped-on 4G modems, 3D-printed boxes) while Izhevsk-built Kupol/Garpiya variants are higher production quality, reflecting two distinct engineering cultures operating on the same weapon chassis.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The 'scrappy vs. polished' dual-track model lets Russia test riskier ideas cheaply at one site while scaling proven designs at the other — a pattern worth watching for in China's or Iran's drone production too.

insights.claim: Russia paid Iran $1.75 billion for a license to produce the Shahed domestically at the Alabuga Special Economic Zone, a facility originally built in 2006 to attract Western investment before pivoting to drone manufacturing once Western firms withdrew at the war's onset.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Repurposed civilian-investment infrastructure becoming wartime drone manufacturing capacity is a template sanctions-focused analysts should track for dual-use industrial zones elsewhere.

themes.theme: Electronic warfare arms race drives antenna scaling

insights.claim: Ukrainian electronic warfare can neutralize nearly half of Geran drones launched in some night attacks, according to a Ukrainian Air Force official in early 2026, forcing Russia into continuous antenna upgrades.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Roughly 50% EW interception rates show Ukrainian counter-drone tech is materially effective, but Russia's antenna race narrative below shows this edge erodes quickly without continuous reinvestment.

insights.claim: Geran antenna element counts grew from 4 (Iranian Nasir) to 8 (Kometa-R8) to 12 (Kometa-M12) to 16-element arrays within about two years (2023-2025), with EW resilience scaling roughly linearly with element count — each added element lets the drone resist one more jamming source.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The antenna-count trajectory is a direct, trackable proxy for the intensity of the Russia-Ukraine EW arms race and a leading indicator of how quickly Chinese CRPA suppliers are iterating for a paying customer.
insights.quote: The antenna counts trace the Ukrainian jamming curve.

insights.claim: China has become the primary external supplier of Geran subsystems (CRPA antenna modules, turbojet engines, mesh radio modems, telemetry modems) after Russia exhausted its original Iranian parts supply, despite China not being a co-belligerent.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Chinese commercial electronics firms (Xingkai Tech, Telefly, ZTE) are de facto arming Russia's drone war — a concrete sanctions/export-control target list for policymakers and a data point for China-Russia dual-use supply chain risk in portfolios.
insights.locator: The Electronic Warfare Arms Race / From Fire-and-Forget to Remote Operator Control

insights.claim: Ukraine's monthly Geran interception rate climbed from 77 percent in February 2024 to 97 percent by May 2024 before Russia responded with a redesigned circular 8-element antenna array by January 2025, illustrating rapid Ukrainian counter-adaptation followed by Russian correction within roughly eight months.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The eight-month correction cycle is a concrete cadence benchmark for how fast an adversary can close a counter-drone effectiveness gap once it identifies the flaw.

themes.theme: From fire-and-forget munition to remote-piloted strike aircraft

insights.claim: The Geran evolved from a fire-and-forget preprogrammed munition into a remotely piloted, loitering strike aircraft after Russia added mesh-radio modems (Xingkai Tech's XK-F358) that turn every drone into a signal repeater, enabling real-time operator control and dynamic rerouting through neighboring nodes if a link is compromised.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: This is a qualitative capability jump — cheap mass-produced drones with mesh-network resilience approach the mission flexibility of much costlier remotely piloted aircraft, changing the cost calculus of air defense.
insights.locator: From Fire-and-Forget to Remote Operator Control

insights.claim: By early 2025 Gerans were flying with standardized telemetry modules (a Raspberry Pi and two Chinese ZTE 3G/LTE modems with both Russian and Ukrainian SIM cards for redundancy) that began as an improvised taped-on 4G modem experiment in November 2023 — the ad hoc modification became a formal subsystem within about 15 months.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A ~15-month path from improvised hack to standardized production subsystem is a concrete benchmark for how fast Russia's wartime innovation cycle formalizes field experiments.
insights.locator: From Fire-and-Forget to Remote Operator Control

insights.claim: Not every experimental modification succeeds and gets standardized — a Geran fitted with a Starlink terminal was downed in September 2024 and never became a serialized solution, unlike the 4G modem approach, showing Russia's process discards failed experiments quickly.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Illustrates that Russia's rapid-iteration model is a genuine test-and-discard engineering process, not indiscriminate mass deployment of every idea — useful context for any US program trying to replicate it.
insights.locator: From Fire-and-Forget to Remote Operator Control

insights.claim: Geran payloads grew from a 118-pound Iranian penetrator warhead to nearly 230-pound combined payloads (Izhevsk stacking two 115-pound BST-52 warheads), while auxiliary munitions like PTM-3 anti-tank mines, R-60 air-to-air missiles, and Verba MANPADS were added for secondary targets and self-defense against interceptors.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Growing payload weight and self-defense armament raises the effective lethality-per-dollar of the Geran platform, a key variable for modeling Ukraine's air-defense cost burden going forward.

insights.claim: In March 2026 a Geran was spotted carrying two first-person-view drones on top of its airframe for mid-flight release, turning the platform into a 'drone mothership' — a minor hardware change (two drone mounts) that fundamentally expanded the platform's battlefield role.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Mothership-configured one-way attack drones could multiply effective strike density per launch, a force-multiplication trend worth monitoring for its impact on Ukrainian (and future NATO) air-defense saturation planning.

themes.theme: Breaking the airframe ceiling: jet-powered Geran-4/5

insights.claim: Modular upgrades to the Geran hit a structural ceiling when Russia tried to add a turbojet engine (Geran-3, using a Chinese Telefly JT80 reaching 300 mph) to the original Iranian piston airframe, which lacked the structural strength to survive the resulting G-loads — forcing Russia to fully redesign the airframe into the Geran-4 and Geran-5.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: This is the clearest evidence that incremental component-swapping has diminishing returns and that platform redesign, not just subsystem iteration, becomes necessary at some threshold — a useful framework for assessing when other iterative weapons programs will need a clean-sheet redesign.

insights.claim: In August 2026 Ukrainian Defense Intelligence reported Russia had halted production of the jet-powered Geran-3 as it reoriented production lines fully around the redesigned Geran-4 and Geran-5, which reach up to 311 mph — a deliberate platform-swap under the same doctrine of constant reinvention.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The Geran-4/5 transition suggests Russia's attack-drone speed will keep climbing, which will further pressure Ukraine's (and any future NATO) point-defense interceptor cost curve and reaction-time requirements.
